script: My sister‑in‑law demanded a full day of free labor, and I…. I was driving home from a long day at work when she texted me. "Hey, I found this playground on FB Marketplace," she wrote, "and it's free. Can you and [husband] pick it up, drive it to my place, and set it up? I'll have lunch at K‑BBQ afterward." The whole thing was a 2‑hour drive, disassemble, haul, reassemble—no help from us, just a full‑day labor gig. I stared at the screen. "No," I typed. She hit me with the sympathy card: "I've been holding down the fort without BIL." I could feel the familiar sting of being the only one in the family who's ever had to step up. "I'll pay $20 for gas," she added, "and you can get us ice cream if we get dinner." I laughed, but it was a cold laugh. "I am not going to do that for free," I said, because I knew the pattern. My husband had finally set boundaries after years of letting his twin brother have us. The twins had always treated us like extras. This was just another one of those insane requests from my sister‑in‑law, who never pays for anything but expects us to do everything. I told her we couldn't. She was like, "Fine, but you're still the only one who can do this." I could hear the audacity in her voice. I thought about how I'd been the one to clean the house, cook, and support her brother when he needed it. I'd never been asked to move a playground for a 10‑year‑old. She sent a follow‑up, "What about a few hours? I'll pick up the truck." I imagined the whole day: a long drive in his truck, hauling a huge set of plastic blocks, wrestling with bolts, and then a half‑hour lunch at K‑BBQ. My stomach dropped. I didn't want to be the one who made it happen for a free lunch that she'd never paid for. I also didn't want to be the one who had to keep the family afloat. I responded with a short, "I am sorry, but no." I could see the disappointment in her eyes. She didn't push back. She just sent a message about how much she appreciated us. I knew she was just trying to make a point. I knew that if I said yes, it would set a precedent for every ridiculous request that followed. I knew I was better at saying no than I was at saying yes to unreasonable demands. I texted her back, "I am not going to do it. Maybe you can ask someone else?" I didn't add anything else. The silence after that was loud. I didn't feel guilty. I felt relieved. I knew I was doing the right thing for my sanity and for the boundaries I had fought so hard to set.
